content: Infections are currently responsible for approximately one-fifth of neonatal deaths worldwide. Early identification and treatment of young infants showing signs of possible serious bacterial infection (PSBI) are critical to reducing mortality and morbidity. A new guideline has been developed to provide simplified antibiotic regimens for treating sick young infants in resource-limited settings where referral care is not feasible or accepted by families. The careful introduction and implementation of this guideline can improve access to treatment, enhance adherence, and ultimately save lives. Effective implementation of the guideline requires countries to strengthen their health systems to ensure high-quality, accessible, and family-friendly care at the first level of health facilities. Ministries of health, international organizations, regional and national medical associations, including pediatric associations, play a vital role in supporting the integration of this guideline into policies and practices. Home visits during the first week after birth are recommended to provide care for mothers and newborns, counsel families, identify danger signs, and promote care-seeking behavior. These visits can be conducted by clinicians, midwives, or trained community health workers (CHWs). However, in settings with high neonatal mortality, hospitalization and life-saving treatment may not always be accessible, acceptable, or affordable for families. Studies in South Asia and Africa indicate that up to two-thirds or more of families do not accept hospital referral for young infants with PSBI. The new WHO guideline addresses care for sick young infants in settings where families cannot access or do not accept referral care. It provides simplified outpatient management options by appropriately trained health workers. In 2015, infections such as sepsis, meningitis, and pneumonia accounted for a significant proportion of the 2.7 million neonatal deaths globally, with South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa bearing a disproportionate burden. The WHO standard for managing PSBI in young infants remains hospital referral for inpatient treatment with a 7to 10-day course of injectable antibiotics (ampicillin or benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin). However, many sick infants are not recognized due to non-specific signs like poor feeding or movement only when stimulated. Home visits in the neonatal period are essential for identifying these signs and ensuring timely care. For young infants aged 0–59 days with PSBI, the guideline recommends referral to a hospital after pre-referral treatment. If referral is not accepted or feasible, outpatient treatment with simplified antibiotic regimens is advised. For infants aged 7–59 days with fast breathing as the only sign of illness, oral amoxicillin twice daily for 7 days is recommended. Hospitalization is not required for these cases. For newborns aged 0–6 days with fast breathing, referral to a hospital is recommended after pre-referral treatment. If referral is refused, oral amoxicillin can be administered by a trained health worker. For young infants with clinical severe infection, two outpatient treatment options are available: 1. Oral amoxicillin twice daily for 7 days plus injectable gentamicin once daily for 7 days. 2. Oral amoxicillin twice daily for 7 days plus injectable gentamicin once daily for 2 days. Option 1 has more evidence supporting its use, but both regimens show similar outcomes. The choice between these options depends on the health system's capacity to provide 7 versus 2 days of injectable antibiotics. For critically ill young infants, pre-referral treatment should be administered, and referral to a hospital is essential. If referral is not feasible, simplified outpatient treatment regimens should be used. Follow-up for infants receiving injectable gentamicin for 7 days should occur daily, while those receiving 2 injections should be followed up on days 2 and 4. The guideline emphasizes the need for national adaptation to suit local social, cultural, and economic contexts. Implementation requires integration into national health strategies and alignment with existing health system interventions, such as the Every Newborn Action Plan. Additional research is needed to improve care for this vulnerable group. National policy development should include advocacy for the guideline, stakeholder discussions for adaptation, distribution of national guidelines, and creating an enabling environment for implementation. Strengthening referral mechanisms, improving care quality and accessibility, and investing in supportive supervision, monitoring, and evaluation are critical. Implementation research is also necessary to optimize the scale-up of PSBI management in young infants when referral care is not accessible.
